claims.text: Suppressing atomic clustering preserves a uniform single-phase structure in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Low atomic size mismatch among constituent elements governs the suppression of atomic clustering.
Low atomic size mismatch minimizes local strain.
Minimizing local strain inhibits chemical segregation.
The initial Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni-variant nanoalloy is uniformly mixed.
The baseline composition has moderate atomic size differences.
Atomic size mismatch can be varied through targeted substitution of one minor element.
The comparison is conducted after annealing at 800–1000 °C under an inert atmosphere.
Differences in local strain caused by atomic size mismatch produce short-range chemical ordering and potentially nanoscale interfacial segregation.
Reduced local strain limits the driving force for atomic clustering.
Larger atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortions.
Increased local distortions promote clustering and phase separation.
Clustering and emergent phase separation compromise structural stability.
Alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch will show significantly less clustering than alloys with larger mismatch after high-temperature annealing.
Alloys with minimal atomic size mismatch will remain single phase more readily than alloys with larger mismatch.
An Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni baseline with moderate size differences is expected to exhibit some short-range clustering at high temperature.
Substantial changes in chemistry or the presence of other stabilizing mechanisms may alter the predicted stability behavior.
Surface or interface energy and entropy contributions may interact with atomic size mismatch in controlling clustering.
XRD, high-resolution TEM, and atom-probe pair-correlation measurements can be used to compare phase separation and clustering across the samples.
Equivalent or greater clustering in the lower-mismatch alloys relative to higher-mismatch alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Both fields say that overall composition is held constant while one element is replaced by another. Elemental substitution necessarily changes chemical composition unless 'overall composition' is narrowly defined as retaining the same total atomic fractions; that definition is not supplied.
